In 1300, the Ottomans ruled a patch of Anatolia so small you could ride across it in two days.

383 years later, their empire stretched from Algeria to the gates of Vienna.

How a border tribe became a superpower — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Around 1299, Osman I led one of a dozen Turkish frontier states left over from the collapsing Seljuk world.

His luck: the frontier faced dying Byzantium. Warriors seeking land and glory flocked to whoever delivered victories.

Osman delivered.

2/ 1354: an earthquake flattens the walls of Gallipoli, and the Ottomans walk into Europe.

1389: Kosovo breaks Serbian power.

1453: Mehmed II, aged 21, takes Constantinople with cannon the Byzantines couldn't answer.

The Roman Empire ends; the map's dark core is complete.

3/ Then the empire doubled in eight years.

Selim I (1512-1520) crushed the Mamluks and took Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina — the huge 1520 band on the map.

The Ottomans now controlled the richest trade routes on Earth and claimed the caliphate itself.

4/ Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566) pushed the frontier to its famous limits: Belgrade 1521, Rhodes 1522, Hungary smashed at Mohács 1526, Vienna besieged 1529, Baghdad taken, North Africa vassalized.

One state now bordered Morocco, Persia and the Holy Roman Empire at once.

5/ The 1683 layer is the high-water mark — and the turning point.

The second siege of Vienna ended with Jan Sobieski's winged hussars breaking the Ottoman army.

By 1699, Hungary was lost. The empire that had only ever expanded began 200 years of retreat.

6/ From two-day ride to three continents — and the borders it drew (Balkans, Middle East, North Africa) still shape the news today.
